> **What you can defend when you leave.** Decide whether this work is ready to leave your hands, and say what the next study should be.

## What this station produces

A release audit, your final dossier, an explicit stopping rule, and your next-study agenda.

This is a **versioned checkpoint**, not a pass. You date it, number it, and
attach the reason for the version. When later evidence changes it, you write
the next version rather than editing the last one, because the sequence of
changes is itself part of your research record.

## The practice

1. {'Run the release audit': 'permissions, disclosure, reproducibility, claim boundaries, and every promise you made to participants.'}
2. {'Assemble the dossier': 'contract versions, evidence registry, permissions, measurement, analysis and claim ledgers, AI ledger, artifacts, package, and revision history.'}
3. {'Write your stopping rule': 'why you are stopping here rather than running one more check, stated as a decision.'}
4. {'Write the next-study agenda': 'the question this work opened, and what you would do differently.'}

## The four rails, here

Four concerns cross every station in this book. At this station they take
these specific forms.

- **Ethics, permissions, and data exposure.** Release is the last point at which a permission problem can still be prevented.
- **Evidence, provenance, and reproducibility.** The dossier is the evidence rail made assemblable.
- **AI activity, verification, and human decisions.** Your AI ledger closes here as a complete record, not a summary.
- **Uncertainty, claim boundary, and revision history.** State what you still do not know as clearly as what you found.

## What sends you back

The next-study agenda is the revisit; a research cycle ends by declaring the next one.
